source.title: TernGrad: Ternary Gradients to Reduce Communication in Distributed Deep Learning
source.authors: W. Wen; Cong Xu; Feng Yan; Chun-Peng Wu; Yan-Dan Wang; Yi-Ran Chen; Hai Helen Li

record.tranche_reason: Tests how stochastic ternary gradient quantization affects training and validation accuracy relative to floating-gradient SGD, using different training settings and model families. It does not directly test memorization capacity or the mapped generalization properties.
record.gate_note: The reported accuracy comparisons are outcomes of applying TernGrad, which changes the training gradients, and thus bear on generalization-related versions where the text compares validation accuracy. The throughput model and cited findings are not rows. Training loss and fraction of zeroed gradients are not test-error comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own held-out accuracy comparisons across batch sizes at fixed epoch budgets on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, including learning-rate scaling and a modified TernGrad recipe. These test V5 in additional training settings. Quantization-versus-floating-gradient comparisons alone do not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that TernGrad can approximately preserve baseline accuracy within the same iterations, sometimes improve AlexNet accuracy, and reduce communication. Large-model training requires recipe adjustments, and GoogLeNet loses less than two percentage points on average. The largest-cluster speed results come from a performance model rather than completed training runs.
record.recipe_differences: The intervention is stochastic ternary gradient quantization with layer-wise scaling and clipping, rather than the original large-batch or generalization interventions. Large-scale comparisons also change dropout and weight decay in the TernGrad recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported accuracy changes with minibatch size and training/model setting; the paper notes TernGrad accuracy depends on clipping, layer-wise ternarizing, dropout ratio and weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: TernGrad generally preserves much of floating-gradient accuracy, with model-dependent losses and recipe adjustments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic ternary gradient communication can substantially reduce gradient precision while approximately preserving held-out accuracy in some classifiers.

record.problems: The accuracy comparisons do not isolate gradient quantization in the ImageNet tables because dropout and weight decay also change. Several MNIST accuracy values are figure-only. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The study evaluates validation accuracy, not explicit train-test error gaps.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying accuracy results were omitted. Throughput results, training-loss curves, gradient sparsity, convergence proofs and cited comparisons were excluded because they do not report the claimed held-out generalization outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random-label held-out performance.
Held-out performance of adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning. Different optimizers are used on different tasks, without the required comparison.
Language models, warmup, isolated effects of normalization or regularization changes, and a controlled comparison isolating longer training. No universal batch-size threshold is established.
An isolated dropout intervention. Dropout changes accompany quantization and sometimes weight-decay changes.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparison with alternative measures. Sharp-minimum explanations are interpretations, not measurements.
Identification and removal of memorized training examples.

missing.what: Explicit batch-size contrasts within each gradient method are needed; the current rows primarily encode quantization contrasts. Split the mixed AlexNet batch-1024 result by method.
AlexNet top-5 batch-size results: floating gradients give 80.56%, 80.73%, and 80.28%; TernGrad gives 80.47%, 80.23%, and 80.25% at batches 256, 512, and 1024 respectively, at equal epochs.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any listed version. V5 verdicts use cross-batch comparisons in the supplied tables, not the extracted within-batch quantization differences. No uncertainty estimates establish statistical significance, and the proposed sharpness mechanism is not directly tested.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training, memorization-capacity comparison or natural-label generalization claim is tested.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

The paper compares Adam and SGD training schemes, but reports no corresponding held-out accuracy comparison by optimizer. Table 1 is described as Adam SGD and does not support assigning results to separate optimizer conditions.

Tests minibatch-size conditions in its TernGrad versus floating-gradient comparisons, but not the general large-batch penalty across image classifiers and language models or the full set of adaptation methods in the version.
Dropout is adjusted as part of the TernGrad recipe; the study does not isolate whether adding dropout lowers test error.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other measure is evaluated against train-test gaps.
No memorized training examples are identified or removed.

rows.operation_detail: TernGrad versus floating gradients; accuracy reported across worker counts.
rows.baseline: floating-gradient baseline; exact values figure only
rows.note: The text says accuracy was similar within the same iterations and gives maximum gain and loss across these experiments, but does not assign those extrema to worker counts.
rows.check: Total batch size remains 64 while worker count changes. This tests gradient quantization and distribution across workers, not a large-batch penalty.

rows.baseline: floating-gradient baseline; exact values figure only
rows.note: The text reports results for both momentum SGD and vanilla SGD together; it does not assign the maximum gain or loss to a specific optimizer.
rows.check: Total batch size remains 64. Comparing vanilla SGD with its quantized counterpart does not test V4 or V5.

rows.subject: CifarNet
rows.note: Both trainings terminate after the same epochs; the reported accuracy difference is less than 1%.
rows.check: This supplies the small-batch reference for R4, not an independently measurable batch-size effect. The optimizer is Adam; 'SGD' is the table's column heading. Record 300K iterations and base learning rate 0.0002.

rows.subject: CifarNet
rows.note: The authors state accuracy degrades under a large minibatch in both baseline and TernGrad.
rows.check: Recast the contrast against batch 128 in R3, separately by gradient method. At equal epochs, floating-gradient accuracy falls from 86.56% to 83.19%, and TernGrad from 85.64% to 82.80%. The extracted within-batch quantization difference is not the V5 effect. Record Adam, 18.75K iterations, and base learning rate 0.0002.
